hero.title: Are you in a relationship with a narcissist?
hero.description: A confidential, caring self-assessment to help you put words on what you're going through.

section1.title: Why do you feel the need to take this test?
section1.p1: Simply looking for a narcissistic partner test is rarely a coincidence. You don't wonder whether you're sharing your life with a manipulator when everything is fine. If you're here, a small voice has been whispering for a while that something is off, without you quite being able to name it.
section1.p2: The heart of a relationship with a narcissist isn't spectacular violence: it's constant doubt. “Am I too sensitive? Am I the problem? Am I overreacting?” This mental fog is no accident: it's exactly the effect manipulation is after, slowly eroding the trust you have in your own perception.
section1.p3: You're looking here for an outside, objective perspective, because from the inside everything blurs together. This test doesn't replace a professional's opinion, but it does separate what belongs to an ordinary toxic relationship from what belongs to genuine coercive control.

section2.title: What exactly is a narcissist (or 'narcissistic pervert')?
section2.p1: The term narcissistic pervert (or covert narcissist), popularised by psychiatrist Marie-France Hirigoyen, describes a person who combines a narcissistic need for domination with a perverse way of relating: they feed on the other, draining their energy and self-esteem, without ever feeling genuine guilt.
section2.p2: Be careful, though, not to slap this label on too quickly. Having an ego, being selfish or going through a rough patch doesn't make someone a narcissist. The difference lies in intent and repetition:
section2.healthy: Someone simply clumsy or self-centred may hurt you without meaning to, but they're able to realise it, apologise sincerely and change their behaviour.
section2.toxic: A narcissist, on the other hand, instrumentalises: the relationship isn't a bond between equals, it's a power struggle in which your suffering counts for nothing against their need for control.
section2.quote: A narcissist doesn't first seek to be loved: they seek to control. And they arrange things so that you carry the blame for the harm they do to you.

section3.title: How to read your result
section3.intro: Each question carries a weight matching what it really reveals, and each answer a value matching its rank. The total runs from 0 to 255 points. Here is how to read your score. Keep in mind this is an indicator, not a diagnosis.
section3.row1Analysis: Your relationship seems built on respect. Tension exists, as everywhere, but not the machinery of coercive control.
section3.row2Level: A few signals to keep an eye on
section3.row2Analysis: A few behaviours deserve your vigilance. Set a clear limit and watch how the other person reacts.
section3.row3Analysis: Several mechanisms of control are in place. It's important to get support and start protecting yourself.
section3.row4Level: A profile strongly suggestive of a narcissist
section3.row4Analysis: The picture is close to narcissistic abuse. Your emotional, even physical, safety must become the priority.

section4.title: The machinery of control: how you fall into the trap
section4.p1: If your score is high, a question may be eating at you: “How could I have let this happen?”. That guilt is unfair. You don't 'choose' to fall under a narcissist's control: you slide into it, through a frighteningly effective process.
section4.p2: Coercive control almost always sets in over three stages:
section4.pillar1Text: At first, it's a fairy tale. Constant attention, compliments, plans for the future, the feeling of having finally found your soulmate. This intense seduction creates a powerful attachment… and a wonderful memory you'll cling to later, when everything goes wrong.
section4.pillar2Text: Once you're attached, the mask slips little by little. A criticism 'for your own good', a dig disguised as a joke, a humiliating comparison. Your threshold of tolerance quietly retreats, and you end up finding 'normal' what you'd never have accepted at the start.
section4.pillar3Text: This is the most powerful trap. A narcissist isn't unpleasant 100% of the time: they alternate hot and cold, moments of fusion and icy breakups. These unpredictable returns of affection act like a drug on the brain and create genuine emotional dependency.

section5.title: The signs that should really alert you
section5.intro: Beyond the score, it's certain specific mechanisms that signal narcissistic abuse. If you recognise several of them, your vigilance is justified. Many overlap, in fact, with the most destructive red flags in a relationship.
section5.pillar1Text: “I never said that”, “you're making it up”, “you're paranoid”. A narcissist denies facts you actually lived through, until you doubt your own memory and judgement. It's a silent form of psychological abuse that attacks your very identity.
section5.pillar2Text: Whatever happens, it's always your fault. They systematically play the victim, turn your grievances back on you, and you end up apologising… for things you didn't do.
section5.pillar3Text: Little by little, your friends 'don't deserve you', your family 'meddles in everything'. A narcissist cuts you off from your support network and monitors your time, your money or who you see, sometimes under the cover of love or jealousy.
section5.pillar4Title: The double face and the lack of empathy
section5.pillar4Text: Charming in public, contemptuous in private: “no one would believe me”. And faced with your pain, all you meet is a disconcerting coldness, sometimes irritation. This real lack of empathy is the signature of a narcissist.

section6.title: The test suggests likely control: what now?
section6.p1: First, remember that this test is a tool for reflection, not a verdict. It never replaces a professional's opinion. If you think you're living in a controlling, even dangerous, relationship, surround yourself with truly competent people.
section6.p2: Becoming aware of the situation is the hardest step, and you've just taken it. A high score doesn't mean 'leave this minute' (except in cases of immediate physical danger), but it does mean the status quo is no longer sustainable. Here's where to start.
section6.dont1Text: You will never be your partner's therapist. Narcissistic perversion is a deep way of functioning that only the person concerned could decide to work on, which is exceedingly rare. Exhausting yourself trying to repair them will only harm you further.
section6.dont2Text: Brandishing this result will almost certainly trigger a crisis, denial or a reversal ('you're the manipulator'). Keep it to yourself, as an inner compass, not as evidence to negotiate.
section6.do1Text: Keep a factual journal of the words and scenes that hurt you. Re-reading, in the cold light of day, what really happened is the best antidote to the doubt gaslighting plants in you.
section6.do2Text: Talk to someone you trust and, ideally, to a professional (a psychologist) or an organisation specialised in psychological abuse. Saying things out loud strips away part of their power.
section6.do3Title: Set a limit and prepare your safety
section6.do3Text: Set a simple, firm limit on an unacceptable behaviour, then observe: a healthy partner adjusts, a narcissist escalates. There are things you should never accept, and you have every right to protect yourself.

section7.title: The takeaway: your gut feeling is a compass
section7.p1: This narcissistic partner test isn't a court verdict: it's a mirror. If you answered these questions with a knot in your stomach, it's because your body already knows what your mind still struggles to admit.
section7.p2: A loving relationship should be a refuge, not a battlefield where you walk on eggshells. The confusion you feel isn't a weakness: it's the sign that you've been trying, for far too long, to adapt to an abnormal situation. You have the right to be respected, heard and safe, which is also what our healthy relationship test measures.
section7.p3: If this result worries you, don't carry this weight alone. Talking to someone is already a first step out of coercive control.

jsonLd.quizDescription: Find out whether your partner shows the signs of a narcissist with this 20-question self-assessment.
jsonLd.faq1Q: How can you recognise a narcissist in a relationship?
jsonLd.faq1A: Recurring signs include love bombing at the start, gradual devaluation, gaslighting (denying your reality), reversed guilt, isolation, control and a lack of empathy in the face of your suffering.
jsonLd.faq2Q: What's the difference between a narcissist and someone who is simply selfish?
jsonLd.faq2A: A selfish or clumsy person can question themselves, apologise and change. A narcissist manipulates intentionally and repeatedly, without real guilt, using the other person as a tool.
jsonLd.faq3Q: Is this narcissistic partner test reliable?
jsonLd.faq3A: It's a tool for reflection and self-assessment, not a medical diagnosis. A high score proves nothing on its own, but it's an invitation to talk to a professional and to protect yourself.
